**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER**

a) Examine the role played by any THREE of the following to trigger floods.

i) Ice and snow thaw (melt)

ii) Tsunamis

iii) Deforestation

iv) Urbanization

(15 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **flood** is the covering of normally dry land by water, usually because a river overflows its banks or the sea invades the coast. Each of the four factors below can trigger floods; **three** are required (5 marks each).

**i) Ice and snow thaw (melt)**

- In cold and mountainous regions water is stored as snow and ice in winter. When the temperature rises quickly in spring, or when warm rain falls on the snow (a rain-on-snow event), the **snow melts rapidly** and releases a large volume of water, often onto **frozen, impermeable ground** that cannot absorb it, so the run-off goes straight to the rivers, which overflow (the spring floods of the rivers of Siberia and of the Red River of the North in the United States and Canada in 1997).
- **Ice jams:** broken river ice piles up and blocks the channel downstream, making the water back up and flood. The melting of glaciers can also **fill glacial lakes that burst their natural dams** (glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalayas), and global warming increases the melting of ice and the risk of such floods and of the rise of the sea level.

**ii) Tsunamis**

- A tsunami is a series of **very long sea waves** produced by a sudden displacement of the sea floor by an **undersea earthquake**, a submarine landslide or a volcanic eruption. In the open ocean the waves are low but very fast; as they reach the **shallow water near the coast** they slow down, rise to great heights, and **surge far inland**, flooding the coastal lowland with a mass of water, sediments and debris, and then retreating.
- The flooding is sudden and devastating: the Indian Ocean tsunami of **December 2004** (generated off Sumatra) killed more than 200 000 people around the ocean, and the **2011 Japan tsunami** flooded large areas of the Tohoku coast. Low-lying coasts, river mouths and flat coastal plains are the most exposed.

**iii) Deforestation**

- Trees **intercept** rainfall, take up water from the soil and release it by **transpiration**, and their roots and the humus layer help **infiltration**. When the forest is cleared, less rainwater is intercepted and infiltrated, and **more runs off the surface** and reaches the rivers quickly: the **lag time shortens** and the **flood peak is higher**.
- The cleared soil is **eroded**, and the silt deposited in the channels and in the reservoirs **raises the river bed** and reduces the capacity of the channel, so the river overflows more easily. Examples: the floods in the Yangtze basin in 1998 were partly blamed on deforestation in the upper basin; deforestation in the highlands increases floods in the lowlands in many tropical countries.

**iv) Urbanization**

- Towns replace the soil and vegetation with **impermeable surfaces** (roofs, roads, pavements, car parks), which prevent infiltration and cause a very large and very fast surface run-off. **Storm drains and gutters** carry the water directly and quickly to the rivers, so the **lag time is short, the peak discharge is high** and floods are more frequent (flash floods).
- Buildings are put on **flood plains and river banks**, in wetlands and in valley bottoms, and **drains are blocked** by waste and are often too small, so water cannot flow away. Examples: the repeated flooding of **Douala** and of **Yaounde** in the rainy season, and of Lagos, Jakarta and Houston.

**Conclusion.** The effect of each factor is to increase the amount or the speed of water reaching a channel or the coast, or to reduce the capacity of the channel to carry it.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Suggest TWO strategies put in place by Cameroon government to mitigate the effect of drought in the Northern part of the Country.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Northern part of Cameroon** (the Adamawa, the North and especially the **Far North**) has a tropical savanna and Sahelian climate with a long dry season, erratic and decreasing rainfall, and recurrent droughts, which cause crop failure, shortage of water and pasture, loss of livestock, food insecurity and migration. Two strategies of the government (5 marks each) are as follows.

**1. Water control: dams, irrigation and the supply of drinking water**

- The government built dams and irrigation schemes to supply water in the dry season: the **Lagdo dam** on the Benue (built in the early 1980s) provides water for irrigation, drinking water and electricity and regulates the flow; the **Maga dam** and the rice-growing schemes of **SEMRY** (in the Yagoua and Maga area) supply irrigation for rice and other crops, even in years of poor rainfall.
- Boreholes, wells and village water points are drilled for people and livestock; small reservoirs and the harvesting of rainwater are encouraged. This reduces the dependence on the rains.

**2. Afforestation and the protection of the environment (fighting desertification)**

- Reforestation programmes such as the **Operation Green Sahel** (Operation Sahel Vert), launched in the late 1980s, plant trees and **windbreaks** and protect the existing vegetation in the Far North to slow down the advance of the desert, reduce the wind and water erosion, protect the soils and improve the local climate.
- Related measures: soil conservation (stone bunds, contour ploughing, planting of grass), control of bush fires and of overgrazing, and the promotion of improved stoves and of other sources of energy to reduce the cutting of firewood.

**Other acceptable strategies** (if a candidate chooses them instead): the promotion of **drought-resistant crops and improved seeds** (sorghum, millet, cowpea, early-maturing varieties) with agricultural research and extension; the building of **cereal banks and food reserves** and the distribution of food aid in bad years; early warning systems; cooperation with the neighbouring countries in the **Lake Chad Basin Commission** to manage the water of the basin; and the help given to herders (water points and pasture management).

**Conclusion.** The government combines the control and storage of water with the protection of the vegetation and soils to make the north less vulnerable to drought, although the results are limited by insufficient resources and by the rapid growth of the population.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR**

a) i) What are Trade Blocs?

(5 marks)

ii) How is visible trade different from invisible trade?

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trade blocs (5 marks)**

A **trade bloc** is a **group of countries**, usually in the same region, that **agree to reduce or remove trade barriers** (tariffs, quotas and other restrictions) **among themselves** in order to increase trade and economic cooperation, and often have a common policy towards the countries outside the group. The degree of integration varies:

1. **Preferential trade area:** members charge lower tariffs on each other's goods.
2. **Free trade area:** no tariffs between members, but each member keeps its own tariffs towards outsiders (the African Continental Free Trade Area, the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement).
3. **Customs union:** a free trade area with a **common external tariff** (CEMAC, the Economic Community of Central African States, is moving in this direction; Mercosur).
4. **Common market:** a customs union with the free movement of **labour and capital** as well as goods.
5. **Economic and monetary union:** a common market with a common economic policy and currency (the European Union and the euro zone; CEMAC and the CFA franc).

Examples: the **European Union**, **ECOWAS**, **CEMAC** (to which Cameroon belongs), **ASEAN**, **Mercosur**. Their aims are to widen the market, to attract investment, to use resources better and to strengthen the bargaining power of members.

**(ii) Visible and invisible trade (5 marks)**

| Point | Visible trade | Invisible trade |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | Trade in **physical goods** that can be seen, touched and counted | Trade in **services and other payments** that have no physical form |
| **Examples** | Crude oil, cocoa, coffee, timber, cotton, bananas, cars, machinery | Banking, insurance, shipping and air transport, tourism, telecommunications, education and consultancy services; income from investments; remittances |
| **Recording** | Recorded by **customs** at the ports and borders | Not recorded at the borders: recorded from the accounts of firms and banks |
| **Balance** | Gives the **balance of trade** (value of visible exports minus visible imports) | Together with the visible trade it gives the **current account** of the balance of payments |

Developing countries such as Cameroon depend mainly on visible exports (primary products), and they often have a deficit in invisible trade (they pay for foreign shipping, insurance and technical services), while developed countries have large surpluses in invisibles (banking and insurance).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) i) State and briefly explain THREE reasons why Cameroon benefits little from international trade?

(9 marks)

ii) Suggest TWO measures that can be adopted by Cameroon to benefit fully from international trade?

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Three reasons why Cameroon benefits little from international trade (9 marks, 3 marks each)**

1. **Dependence on a few primary products with low and unstable prices.** Cameroon exports mainly raw materials (crude oil, cocoa, coffee, cotton, bananas, timber, rubber), whose prices on the world market are **low and fluctuate widely**, while it imports **expensive manufactured goods, machinery and fuel products**. The **terms of trade** therefore tend to worsen: more exports must be sold to buy the same quantity of imports, and the earnings of farmers and of the country are unstable.
2. **A narrow export base and little processing (low value added).** The export raw materials leave the country unprocessed (logs, raw cocoa, cotton fibre), so most of the **value added**, the jobs and the profits of processing are gained by the importing countries. There are few industries to make the goods that the country needs, so it has a **trade deficit** in manufactured goods.
3. **Poor infrastructure and high costs, and weak competitiveness.** Bad roads and railways, congestion at the port of Douala, delays at the borders, power cuts, red tape, corruption and smuggling raise the cost of production and exports; low productivity, the lack of capital and technology, and the inability to meet the **quality standards** of the rich markets, restrict the competitiveness of Cameroonian goods.
4. (Other acceptable reasons) **trade barriers and subsidies** of the developed countries (agricultural subsidies in the European Union and the United States), the **concentration of trade with a few partners**, the dependence on foreign companies that repatriate profits, and the competition from cheap imported goods.

**(ii) Two measures to benefit fully (6 marks, 3 marks each)**

1. **Diversify and add value to the exports.** Develop the **processing of local raw materials** (cocoa into chocolate and butter, timber into furniture and sawn wood, cotton into textiles, fruit into juice) and encourage the export of **manufactured and semi-finished goods**, new crops and services (tourism); this raises the income, creates jobs and reduces the dependence on a few products and on the fluctuation of prices.
2. **Improve the infrastructure and the trade environment, and widen markets through regional integration.** Build and maintain roads, railways, ports (the deep-sea port of Kribi) and power supply; simplify customs and administrative procedures and fight corruption and smuggling; improve the quality of goods to meet international standards; and make full use of **CEMAC and the African Continental Free Trade Area** to widen the market and to negotiate better terms of trade.
3. (Other acceptable measures) training of the labour force, support to farmers and exporters (credit and market information), and the negotiation of fairer trade agreements.
